title: Reproduce with a message you control, and note there's no error anywhere
explanation: `logger -p local0.info 'test message'` produces no error, but `/var/log/app/app.log` never receives the line. rsyslog isn't crashing or refusing anything — which means it's worth checking whether it's doing exactly what it's configured to do, rather than assuming something is broken.

title: Read the rules in the order rsyslog actually evaluates them
explanation: `cat /etc/rsyslog.d/10-app.conf` shows two rules for `local0`: one routing to `/dev/null` followed by `& stop`, then the real rule filing to `/var/log/app/app.log`. rsyslog evaluates rules top-to-bottom, per message — order isn't cosmetic, it's the entire logic.

title: Understand what `& stop` actually does
explanation: `& stop` halts all further rule processing for any message that matched the rule immediately above it. Since the `/dev/null` rule matches every `local0` message and is followed by `& stop`, the second rule — the one that would actually write to `app.log` — never runs at all for these messages.

title: Recognize the comment as the real explanation, not just documentation
explanation: The `# TEMP: quieting local0 during an investigation -- REMOVE ME` comment above the rule confirms this was a deliberate, temporary debugging measure to silence a noisy facility — never cleaned up afterward. A `stop` short-circuit like this is a very deliberate landmine: useful for genuinely dropping noise, dangerous if left in place.

title: Remove the short-circuit and reload rsyslog's rules
explanation: Replace the file's contents with just the real rule (`local0.*    /var/log/app/app.log`), then restart rsyslog so it re-reads its config — `sudo pkill rsyslogd` followed by `sudo rsyslogd`, since there's no systemd or init script managing it in this environment.

title: Verify with a fresh message, not old data
explanation: `logger -p local0.info 'confirm fix'` followed by `tail /var/log/app/app.log` now shows the new line, confirming messages reach the file rather than being discarded before the real rule ever runs.
